overview: This file assembles American consular reporting and translated official accounts concerning the finances of Japan’s Kwantung Leased Territory and its successor administrative body, the Kwantung Bureau, from 1933 through 1938. It documents annual and supplementary budgets, taxation, loans and public bonds, state enterprises, the opium monopoly, public works, communications, police, and education, while repeatedly tracing ostensibly civilian expenditures to the Kwantung Army, the South Manchuria Railway, the Manchurian occupation, and the war in China. Comparative budgets for 1933–34, 1935–36, and 1938–39 show the reorganization of Japanese administration in Manchuria, the consequences of ending extraterritoriality in Manchukuo, and the growing use of special taxes and transfers to military accounts. The final cross-reference points to a related 1938 report on Manchuria’s international balance of payments.

subfiles.title: Despatch on the Kwantung Government budget for 1933–34
subfiles.from: John Carter Vincent, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports and analyzes the proposed 1933–34 budget of the Kwantung Government.
subfiles.summary: Vincent reports a balanced budget of ¥25,864,792, approximately ¥3.13 million above the preceding year, supported by higher taxation, loans or public bonds, and an increased Japanese government grant. He discusses opium-monopoly income omitted from the published revenue accounts and argues that the territory was more nearly self-supporting than commonly believed. Extraordinary appropriations supported aviation meteorology, salt production, communications, the South Manchuria Railway, and police operations in Manchuria, including improved weapons. The despatch concludes that the budget reveals the blurred financial and administrative boundaries among the Kwantung Government, Kwantung Army, and South Manchuria Railway Company.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs memorandum on the supplementary Kwantung budget
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Summarizes a Dairen despatch reporting a ¥158,000 supplementary appropriation to the Kwantung Government budget.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum notes that the supplementary budget raised the previously reported budget of roughly ¥26 million by ¥158,000. Its largest component was ¥110,000 for military postal service.

subfiles.title: Despatch on the ¥158,000 supplementary budget
subfiles.from: John Carter Vincent, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports a supplementary 1933–34 Kwantung budget financed by bonds or a direct loan.
subfiles.summary: The supplementary budget authorizes ¥20,000 for control of exchange operations, ¥110,000 for military postal service, and ¥28,000 for loan interest and related expenses. Vincent states that bonds or a direct loan would finance the total of ¥158,000, raising overall expenditure and revenue estimates to ¥26,022,792.

subfiles.title: Duplicate copy of the supplementary-budget despatch
subfiles.from: John Carter Vincent, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador at Tokyo
subfiles.about: A retained duplicate of the despatch concerning the supplementary 1933–34 budget.
subfiles.summary: This copy repeats the appropriations for exchange control, military postal service, and loan expenses and states that they would be financed by bonds or borrowing. Its opening figure reads ¥150,000, although the listed items and subsequent statements total ¥158,000, indicating a copying or OCR discrepancy.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of the Kwantung Bureau budget despatch
subfiles.from: Joseph W. Ballantine, American Consul General at Mukden
subfiles.about: Forwards a copy of a despatch to the American Legation at Peiping concerning the Kwantung Bureau budget.
subfiles.summary: Ballantine transmits to the Department of State a copy of his Despatch No. 125, sent the same day to the Legation at Peiping. The enclosure concerns the annual budget of the recently organized Kwantung Bureau.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 125 on the first annual Kwantung Bureau budget
subfiles.from: Joseph W. Ballantine, American Consul General at Mukden
subfiles.to: Nelson Trusler Johnson, American Minister at Peiping
subfiles.about: Analyzes the first annual budget of the reorganized Kwantung Bureau.
subfiles.summary: The despatch explains that the Kwantung Bureau had assumed responsibility for Japanese government establishments in Manchuria, including the leased territory and certain services in the South Manchuria Railway Zone. Its budget balanced at ¥24,738,165, with higher taxes and carryover surpluses but a reduced National Treasury grant. Major expenditures included police, communications, education, grants, and costs associated with the Manchuria Incident, which Ballantine suggests may have contributed to maintenance of the Kwantung Army.

subfiles.title: Translated Kwantung Bureau budget for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1936
subfiles.from: Kwantung Bureau Gazette, translated by the American Consulate General at Mukden
subfiles.about: Provides detailed revenue and expenditure schedules for the Kwantung Bureau budget.
subfiles.summary: The translated schedule gives total revenue of ¥24,738,165, divided between ordinary receipts and extraordinary sources such as property sales, a special profits tax, a Treasury grant, and the previous year’s surplus. It itemizes ordinary expenditure for administration, courts, police, education, the monopoly, communications, pensions, and other services, together with extraordinary undertakings and Manchuria Incident expenses. A concluding provision authorizes up to ¥700,000 in commitments for raw opium oil against the 1936–37 Treasury budget.

subfiles.title: Despatch on the Kwantung Bureau budget for fiscal 1938–39
subfiles.from: William T. Turner, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Analyzes the Kwantung Bureau’s 1938–39 budget and estimates the portion attributable to war in China.
subfiles.summary: Turner reports that the abolition of extraterritoriality in Manchukuo removed the Bureau’s authority over police, judicial, postal, and telegraph affairs in the South Manchuria Railway Zone, producing an apparent budget decline to approximately ¥23.02 million. Ordinary revenues depended heavily on income and other taxes, communications, and opium-monopoly profits, while new wartime taxes replaced declining Treasury subsidies and prior-year surpluses. The principal extraordinary item was a transfer to the temporary military-expenses account, supplemented by air-defense, tax-collection, and national-spirit mobilization appropriations. Turner identifies approximately ¥4.64 million—nearly one-fifth of estimated spending—as readily recognizable military expenditure connected with the Sino-Japanese hostilities.

subfiles.title: Enclosure No. 1: regular Kwantung Bureau budget for 1938–39
subfiles.from: Kwantung Bureau Gazette, translated by William T. Turner
subfiles.about: Presents the detailed regular budget ratified on March 16, 1938.
subfiles.summary: The enclosure itemizes ordinary revenue from taxes, official enterprises, government property, stamps, and miscellaneous receipts, along with extraordinary receipts from property sales, wartime taxes, subsidies, and the previous year’s surplus. Expenditures cover Bureau administration, judiciary, police, education, the opium monopoly, communications, public works, waterworks, land reclamation, subsidies, exchange control, ideological policing, and technical or economic investigations. The schedule also records large transfers to the special account for temporary military expenses and other costs associated with the North China Incident.

subfiles.title: Enclosure No. 2: supplementary Kwantung Bureau budget ratified March 22, 1938
subfiles.from: Kwantung Bureau Gazette, translated by William T. Turner
subfiles.about: Lists supplementary revenues and expenditures, chiefly new taxes and a military-account transfer.
subfiles.summary: The supplementary revenue schedule includes additional income tax and several new imposts on interest, distributed profits, securities, traffic, admissions, and commodities. Ordinary spending is assigned to Bureau administration and communications, while ¥724,164 is transferred to the special account for temporary military expenses. As reproduced here, the revenue and expenditure portions do not balance on their own, a point addressed by the following enclosure.

subfiles.title: Enclosure No. 3: additional portion of the supplementary budget
subfiles.from: Kwantung Bureau, translated by William T. Turner
subfiles.about: Supplies additional expenditure items belonging to the March 1938 supplementary budget.
subfiles.summary: This schedule adds ¥21,740 in ordinary expenditure and ¥159,302 in extraordinary spending. The extraordinary items cover new enterprises, excise administration, commodity and sales investigations, special police undertakings, and temporary aid to local firms. An editorial note explains that this appears to be part of the March 22 supplementary budget and must be combined with it to resolve the apparent imbalance.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Turner’s report on Manchuria’s balance of payments
subfiles.about: Directs researchers to another decimal-file location for a report on Manchuria’s international balance of payments.
subfiles.summary: The sheet refers to Despatch No. 55 from Dairen, dated November 9, 1938, filed at 893.51 Manchuria/97. That report concerned an officially sourced schedule of Manchuria’s balance of international payments, including the Kwantung Leased Territory, obtained at Hsinking.

interest: The file is especially useful for tracing how Japanese colonial administration presented civilian budgets while channeling substantial resources toward policing, railway-zone control, army support, and the expanding war in China. Its detailed schedules expose the fiscal importance of opium, state enterprises, special wartime taxes, bond finance, and transfers to military accounts. The sequence also captures institutional change—from the Kwantung Government to the Kwantung Bureau and then the loss of Railway Zone functions after the abolition of extraterritoriality—while duplicate copies and supplementary enclosures reveal discrepancies and practical problems in reconstructing official totals.
